clue.text: Workers' organisation losing heart after upset disturbing the toffs?

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the letters bottom to top, so they read backwards
the central letter of the word is dropped, as a body losing its heart

parts.note: a trade union is an organisation of workers

explanation.surface: A trade union, half-hearted after a setback, sets out to unsettle the upper classes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing heart' takes the middle I from UNION, leaving UNON; 'upset' turns that round. NON-U is the British label for speech or habits the upper class thinks common.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-U behaviour is what upper-class people regard as vulgar, so it would ruffle posh sensibilities.

clue.text: Raymond's name held in little credit

definitions.note: Raymond Chandler was the American crime novelist who created Philip Marlowe

indicators.note: the name is held inside the short form for credit, as goods held in a box

parts.note: CR is the short form of credit in accounts
a handle is slang for a person's name

explanation.surface: Someone called Raymond is thought little of, his name carrying scant credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond is the first name of the crime writer, so the surname completes him.

clue.text: Cure can be effected by this priest and team, right?

definitions.text: Cure can be effected by this

parts.note: Eli is the priest of the Old Testament who raised Samuel
XI, eleven in Roman numerals, is a cricket or football team

explanation.surface: A healing seemingly worked by a clergyman together with his side.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a supposed cure-all potion, the remedy that heals.

clue.text: You see this as prisoner escapes down drainpipe? Speak haughtily!

parts.note: a con is slang for a convict
an escaping convict shinning down a drainpipe descends

explanation.surface: A picture of a jailbreak down a drainpipe, followed by a rebuke for snootiness.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paints the escape itself: the prisoner climbing down is a CON who DESCENDs.
explanation.definitionFit: To condescend is to talk down to someone with an air of superiority.

clue.text: Idiot — the man had to be dressed

parts.note: a clot is a British word for a fool
he refers to a man
'd is the contraction of had

explanation.surface: A fool and his companion had to get properly attired.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothed and dressed are synonyms, both meaning wearing clothes.

clue.text: Tiniest of roles? Happened to get nothing more

parts.note: to come about is to happen, so came is happened
O, the zero, is nothing

explanation.surface: An actor in the smallest of parts finds nothing more came of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a brief appearance by a performer, often a famous one.

clue.text: Sort of dog in demand I don't fancy

indicators.note: fancy here means elaborate or reworked, so the letters are set out anew

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone says a certain breed is popular, but they do not care for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' is the anagram signal, misdirecting as the verb 'like'. The Dandie Dinmont is a Scottish terrier named after a character in Walter Scott.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dandie Dinmont is a breed of terrier, so it is one sort of dog.

clue.text: Toilets by back of store falling apart?

parts.note: loos is British slang for toilets

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: The lavatories behind a shop are crumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something loose is coming free, close to falling to pieces.

clue.text: Going down without leader brings agitation of mind

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, which is dropped

parts.note: demotion is going down in rank

explanation.surface: Being demoted with no boss leaves someone mentally upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without leader' strips the D from DEMOTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotion is a strong feeling, a stirring or disturbance of the mind.

clue.text: Attack male dog taken into home

indicators.note: the male dog is put inside the word for home

parts.note: in means at home
a pug is a small breed of dog

explanation.surface: A male dog brought indoors goes on the attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To impugn is to challenge or call into question, a verbal attack.

clue.text: Upcoming party to be given by men very close by

parts.note: next means the one coming up
a do is a party
OR, other ranks, are the ordinary soldiers or men

explanation.surface: A forthcoming party is to be laid on by soldiers living nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: Next door means in the adjacent house, so extremely near.

clue.text: Plaything direly befouled with soot

indicators.note: befouled suggests spoilt and messed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A child's toy filthily covered in soot.
explanation.definitionFit: A toy soldier is a small model figure for children to play with.

clue.text: Design trip roughly when the flowers come out

indicators.note: roughly hints at an approximate, scrambled arrangement of the letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Planning an outing loosely for the season of blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Springtide is a poetic word for springtime, the season of blossoming.

clue.text: Wartime general in his limousine

indicators.note: in shows the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A commander travelling in his limousine during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: William Slim was a British field marshal who led the Fourteenth Army in Burma in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: General Slim commanded British forces in Burma during the Second World War.

clue.text: US author as trendier guest abroad

indicators.note: abroad suggests going out of place, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American writer appears as a fashionable visitor overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude Stein was an American writer and Paris salon hostess.

clue.text: Report of sticky stuff with batter being offered as food

indicators.note: report signals a word heard rather than seen

parts.note: goo is sticky stuff
to lash is to beat or batter

explanation.surface: Something gluey mixed with batter is served up as a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'batter' looks like cooking but is the verb, beat: LASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Goulash is a Hungarian stew of meat and paprika, a dish to eat.

clue.text: Spelling a word for 'rubbish' can produce a terrible headache

parts.note: sp is the proofreader's abbreviation for spelling
litter is rubbish

explanation.surface: Getting a word for rubbish wrong is enough to cause a migraine.
explanation.definitionFit: A splitter is informal for a splitting headache, a very bad one.

clue.text: Stream poet observed endlessly

parts.note: Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet

explanation.surface: A poet watched a stream without end.
explanation.definitionFit: Burn is a Scottish word for a small stream or brook.

clue.text: Bradman having failure with the bat seen as comic figure?

parts.note: Sir Donald Bradman was the great Australian cricketer
a duck in cricket is a score of nought

explanation.surface: The great batsman out for nought looks a figure of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: A DUCK is a batsman's score of zero in cricket; Bradman famously made one in his last Test innings.
explanation.definitionFit: Donald Duck is the Disney cartoon character, a comic-strip and screen figure.

clue.text: Businessperson who loses heart several times?

definitions.meaning: a trader who buys and sells goods
at cards, the person who hands out the pack gives away hearts again and again

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the card player who distributes the cards, parting with every heart in the pack.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer is a trader in goods, and at cards the one who hands them round.

clue.text: Maybe the bishop's home is here, not a hundred miles away

definitions.text: Maybe the bishop's home is here
definitions.meaning: the enclosed grounds round a cathedral, where clergy houses stand
a jokey way of saying near

explanation.walkthrough: A cathedral close is the precinct around a cathedral, where the bishop's palace often stands.
explanation.definitionFit: A close is a cathedral precinct; as an adjective it means near.

clue.text: Asian got confused in South American city

indicators.note: confused signals the letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Asian visitor gets lost in a South American city.
explanation.definitionFit: Santiago is the capital of Chile.

clue.text: What can be pulled in body making fellow number at first

definitions.text: What can be pulled in body

indicators.note: at first places the number ahead of the fellow

parts.note: ten is a number
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: A man's body making a numbered appearance.
explanation.definitionFit: A tendon joins muscle to bone and is a common thing to strain or pull.

clue.text: Accountant's gross? No!

parts.note: an accountant's figure that is not the gross is the one left after deductions

explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling with two Ts is the opposite of gross in accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: A net figure is the amount after deductions, the counterpart of gross.

clue.text: Hard border that may separate neighbours

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A tough boundary dividing those next door.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedge is a row of bushes often planted as a boundary between gardens.

clue.text: You will have fantastic art in entertainment building

indicators.note: will have means the word for you holds the other letters inside

parts.note: thee is an old form of you

indicators.note: fantastic suggests fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: You will see wonderful art at a venue for shows.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'in' as the container, but it is only a link: 'will have' does the enclosing, with 'fantastic' scrambling art; 'you' takes its archaic, biblical form.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre is a building where plays and shows are staged.
